updates.name: Hotel Chelsea
updates.fact: Longtime manager Stanley Bard was known for accepting art from struggling artists in place of rent.

updates.name: Hotel Theresa
updates.fact: It stopped operating as a hotel in the 1960s and was converted to offices.

updates.name: Algonquin Hotel
updates.fact: E. B. White wrote his 1948 essay Here Is New York while staying at the hotel.

updates.name: Gramercy Park
updates.fact: The gates traditionally open to the public for carolers on Christmas Eve, one of the few times outsiders can step inside.

updates.name: 30 Rockefeller Plaza
updates.fact: Construction workers put up the first Christmas tree here in 1931. The official tree lighting began in 1933.

updates.name: Macy's Herald Square
updates.fact: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, first held in 1924, ends in front of the store.

updates.name: McSorley's Old Ale House
updates.fact: Dusty wishbones hang over the bar. Legend says soldiers hung them before leaving for World War I, and the ones left belonged to men who never came back.

updates.name: Katz's Delicatessen
updates.fact: During World War II its slogan was "Send a salami to your boy in the army," and it still ships salamis today.

new.name: Church of the Holy Communion
facts: Consecrated in 1846 as an Episcopal church, designed by Richard Upjohn, who also designed Trinity Church.
In the 1980s it became the Limelight, one of the city's most famous nightclubs.
It has since been converted to shops and a gym.

new.name: Puck Building
facts: Built in 1886 to print Puck, a popular humor magazine.
A gilded statue of the character Puck still stands over the entrance.
The old printing plant now holds offices, shops and penthouse homes added on the roof.

new.name: Engine Company 31
facts: Built in 1895 as a firehouse, designed to look like a French Renaissance chateau.
After the fire company moved out in the 1970s, it became home to the Downtown Community Television Center.

new.name: Scribner Building
facts: Built in 1913 as the headquarters and bookstore of Charles Scribner's Sons, the publisher of Hemingway and F. Scott Fitzgerald.
The bookstore closed in 1989. Its landmarked glass-and-iron storefront now holds other shops.

new.name: 454 West 20th Street
facts: In April 1951 Jack Kerouac typed the first full draft of On the Road here, on one long roll of paper, in about three weeks.

new.name: 337 Bleecker Street
facts: Lorraine Hansberry wrote A Raisin in the Sun while living here in the 1950s.

new.name: 53rd & 3rd
facts: The Ramones named their 1976 song "53rd & 3rd" for this intersection.

new.name: Queensboro Bridge
facts: It opened in 1909 and is also known as the 59th Street Bridge.
Simon & Garfunkel named "The 59th Street Bridge Song (Feelin' Groovy)" for it in 1966.
